title: Are exams getting easier?
author: Daisy Christodoulou
summary: Daisy Christodoulou asks whether exams are getting easier and grades inflated, and argues that the question is hard to answer because difficulty cannot be judged from a paper alone and syllabuses change. She describes a 2016 study that used Comparative Judgement on archived A-level pure maths scripts from 1964, 1968, 1996, and 2012. The study found standards were stable between 1964 and 1968 and between 1996 and 2012, but fell between 1968 and 1996. She adds her own suggested cause, the expansion of the A-level cohort. Her main move is to separate grade inflation from underlying attainment, using a worked example and an economics analogy to show that grades are misleading as measures of ability. She closes by calling for national exams to be reported on a consistent underlying scale.
points: Exam difficulty cannot be read off a paper; it needs data on how students responded, which is why cross-era comparisons are hard.
Comparative Judgement of archived scripts showed that the quality of work earning an E in 1968 earned a B in 1996, evidence that A-level maths grade inflation is real.
The author suggests the growth in A-level entry from about 5-10 percent of students to about half the cohort as one explanation for the shift.
Grade inflation does not show pupils are doing worse, because grades sit on top of underlying attainment scales and can diverge from them.
Reporting major exams on a consistent underlying scale would make year-on-year standards visible.
quotes: Even if you do look at two exams and decide that one is much harder than the other, even that gut instinct judgement doesn't tell you that much, because it may well be that students did very badly on the hard exam and much better on the easier exam.

They then used Comparative Judgement to assess the quality of each question response. Comparative Judgement is an innovative assessment technique which relies on the fact that humans are much better at making comparative judgements than absolute ones.
Standards declined between 1968 and 1996. The quality of work that would have produced an E in 1968 would have got a B in 1996.

A-levels in general were taken by about 5-10% of students in the 1960s. Today, about half the cohort take them, and a lot of that increase happened between 1968 and 1996. Keeping the gradeset at the same standard after such an expansion in numbers would mean a large chunk of students failing the exam.

I think this paper shows that grade inflation, for maths A-level at least, is real. The standard represented by a B grade maths in 1996 was not as difficult as the standard represented by a B-grade 30 years earlier.

What I want to show with the above is that grades can be very misleading. They are essentially layered on top of underlying attainment scales, and yet very often we take them as direct measures of underlying attainment.

I would like to see some of the bigger national exams reported on a consistent underlying scale, which would make it easier to see what was happening to standards year on year. Comparative Judgement could play a part in making that happen.
